item.title: Does Leadership Training Change People?
item.description:
Leadership

Does Leadership Training Change People?

The case for a different leadership development paradigm.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Leadership training does not lead to behavior changes in attendees.
  • Behavior changes require regular learning, reflection, practice and repetition.
  • A Continuous Leadership Practice enables people to absorb, practice and implement specific lessons over time.
Leadership training does not change leadership behavior.
Source: THANANIT / Adobe Stock

I am going to come right out and say it:

“Leaders are not developed by attending a leadership training course.”

As provocative as the statement may be, I stand by it. After more than three decades of high-end management consulting and leadership coaching at some of the largest organizations on the planet, I can tell you sending someone to a leadership training session for a week does not a leader make!

Sure, a training course can raise awareness. Some even provide some scenario-based practice sessions. However, by day three back at work, the leader has already defaulted back to their “natural” habits and rituals for leading, making the training they received a fond memory.

Why we think we can help people change by sending them to a training course for a few days is beyond me. Does a single week of education ever lead to deep and lasting change? Not really, because knowing what to do is not the same as doing it.

Yet, according to a special report by Fortune magazine:[i] "The global corporate leadership training market size is valued at $39.59 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow from $42.92 billion in 2026 and reach $73.67 billion by 2034

Why do organizations make such a heavy investment in something that is unlikely to move the needle? While this piece is not intended to address the organizational psychology of poor training investments, my hunch is the answer to this question lies in one of two reasons:

  1. We have always done it this way;

and;

  1. There are no other options.

Regardless, leaders are not created by sending people to a training course.

But there is a better way to create a community of leaders.

The Continuous Leadership Practice Approach

It is my firm belief that people need the time and space to

  • learn
  • reflect
  • practice
  • repeat
  • change

It is a cycle that I call the “Continuous Leadership Practice Approach to Behavioral Change.”

I use it with my leadership coaching clients and it works.

As already mentioned, knowing what to do is not the same as doing it. However, by creating an opportunity for leaders to put their newfound leadership knowledge into practice on a regular basis throughout the week, we help them develop new behaviors.

article continues after advertisement

Indeed, we help them change.

Making The Case for Continuous Leadership Practice

Here’s why the Continuous Leadership Practice Approach to Behavioral Change works:

  1. New Knowledge Is Better Absorbed in Small Increments: A multi-day training class covers a lot of ground. As such, there’s only so much time for reflection and practice before the instructor moves on to the next topic. More is forgotten than retained.

    However, by offering new leadership knowledge in smaller portions and in regular increments, we provide people the time and space needed to truly learn and put new behaviors into practice.

  2. Reflection Is More Important to Behavior Change Than Instruction: Training helps people identify what they should know; reflection helps them decide what that knowledge means for them. Stated another way: without reflection, knowledge is just the accumulation of facts.

    Reflection provides a leader the time they need to create the context in which new knowledge will be applied. The application of the knowledge is, of course, unique for each person. This is reflected in the new behavior that results.

  3. New Behaviors Need Repetition and Feedback: With repetition, the new knowledge slowly becomes part of a person’s leadership repertoire, and that’s when the magic truly happens.

    Results achieved through the new behavior provides the feedback. Behavior is adjusted and repeated. Improvements are made and personal changes transpire.

How To Implement Continuous Leadership Practice

As the name implies, Continuous Leadership Practice Approach to Behavioral Change isn’t something that is accomplished in a week’s training session. Rather, it is a continuous process, and change in leadership skills and behavior is achieved over time.

Here’s how to implement the Continuous Leadership Practice process:

  1. Provide your leaders with specific, bite-sized leadership lessons every week.
  2. Deliver a series of simple exercises that reinforce the key elements of each week’s lesson.
  3. Allow time throughout the week for your leaders to learn, reflect, and practice the work included in the exercises.
  4. Monitor progress. We don’t want lessons delivered each week only to have your leaders ignore them or not complete the exercises.

Here’s an example, from the Indispensable Leadership system[ii] that I am building and will release in the next few weeks, of what might be delivered to leaders each week:

Sample Lesson

You must choose to lead each day.

You don’t lead because of title or position. You lead through behavior.

Role-specific guidance:

Executives: Set the tone for what exceptional leadership looks like by choosing to actively lead your team each day.

Middle Managers: Own the responsibility to lead by doing what is needed to set direction and manage the changes that transpire as your team goes about executing the mission of the organization.

Supervisors: Demonstrate that leadership is more than a title. Be the kind of leader who is present by actively participating in the work at hand.

article continues after advertisement

This Week's Exercises

  1. Leadership Is a Daily Choice

Think about the last 48 hours at work:

1. What is one specific moment when you could have stepped forward to lead—but didn’t?

2. What stopped you?

3. What would “choosing to lead” have looked like in that moment?

Learning: The moments when you hesitate to lead often reveal your greatest opportunities for growth as a leader.

  1. Leadership shows up through behavior, not title.

List two visible actions you took recently that signaled leadership to your team. Examples might include:

1. Setting direction

2. Making a decision others were avoiding

3. Supporting someone who needed guidance

4. Addressing a problem directly, ask yourself: Did people clearly see me leading?

Leadership takeaway: Leadership opportunities appear every day—often in small moments. The leaders who earn trust are the ones who consistently step forward when those moments appear.

3. Leadership requires daily commitment.

1. Identify one leadership behavior you will intentionally demonstrate tomorrow.

2. Complete this sentence: “Tomorrow I will choose to lead by __________________________.”

3. Make it something observable that your team will notice.

Leadership insight: Leadership isn’t proven when it’s convenient—it’s proven in the moments when you choose to step forward instead of stepping back.

article continues after advertisement

As you can see in this example, the lesson is succinct and easy to understand. The exercises address the core principle of the lesson and can be accomplished in just a few minutes per day over the course of a week.

Assuming the next lesson builds on this one, over a month’s time, a leader will have received four or five simple leadership lessons and had 12-15 opportunities to practice and reinforce these lessons through each week’s exercises.

To close, organizations should stop squandering precious resources by sending their people to leadership training sessions—they simply do not help people change their behavior.

Instead, organizations should consider implementing a Continuous Leadership Practice process that enables personnel to absorb specific, bite-sized leadership lessons every week and reflect upon and practice those lessons by completing a set of related (and easy to do) exercises that reinforce key elements of the lesson.

When we do this, we create an environment that can cultivate true change in the way our people lead others—and isn’t that what we want to “train” our leaders to do?
